---
title: "Unitary Matrices — Transform Without Losing Probability"
description: "A compact linear-algebra lesson with mathematical definitions, real values and reasoning."
---

## Start with a question

If a quantum gate changes a state vector, what mathematical property prevents its probability total from exceeding 100%?

## Understand the central idea

A unitary matrix preserves vector length in complex space. That is the mathematical reason quantum gates on closed systems preserve total probability.

## Express it with mathematics

$$
U^\dagger U=I,\qquad\|U\psi\|^2=\|\psi\|^2
$$

**Every symbol explained:** U is a quantum gate matrix; U† means conjugate transpose; I is the identity matrix; ψ is a state vector; ||·||² means sum of squared amplitude magnitudes.

**Substitute real numbers:** The bit-flip gate X=[[0,1],[1,0]] sends input ψ=(1,0) to (0,1). Both vectors have squared norm 1²+0²=1; the gate switched outcomes without creating probability.

## Why this works

For any state ψ, squared norm of Uψ is ψ†U†Uψ=ψ†Iψ=ψ†ψ. The middle substitution uses the unitary condition. This is a proof for every input, not merely one example.

## What can go wrong?

Measurement is not generally a unitary reversible operation, and real quantum devices have noise. Do not confuse unitary evolution with the whole physical process.

## Your turn

Show directly that applying the X gate twice restores input (1,0).
